title: Mapped Types, Keyof & Essential Utility Types
summary: Master mapped types ([K in keyof T]), index access types, and built-in utility types: Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Record.
learningObjectives: Deconstruct and implement built-in utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record) using mapped type syntax
Construct custom mapped types that enforce immutability or transform property types systematically

sections.heading: 1. Mapped Types Syntax & Built-in Utility Architecture
sections.content:
Mapped types allow you to create new types based on existing types by iterating over their properties—similar to `Array.prototype.map()`, but for type definitions.

Mapped Type Syntax:
`type Mapped<T> = { [K in keyof T]: TransformedType };`

How Built-in Utility Types are Implemented Under the Hood:
1. `Partial<T>`: Makes all properties optional (`?` modifier):
`type Partial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };`
2. `Required<T>`: Removes optionality (`-?` modifier):
`type Required<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };`
3. `Readonly<T>`: Freezes all properties (`readonly` modifier):
`type Readonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };`
4. `Record<K, T>`: Creates a dictionary mapping keys `K` to value type `T`:
`type Record<K extends keyof any, T> = { [P in K]: T };`
5. `Pick<T, K>`: Extracts a subset of properties from `T`:
`type Pick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] };`
6. `Omit<T, K>`: Constructs a type with all properties except `K`:
`type Omit<T, K extends keyof any> = Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>;`

Modifiers:
- `+readonly` or `-readonly` adds or strips immutability.
- `+?` or `-?` adds or strips optionality.

codeExamples.code:
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| MAPPED TYPES & UTILITY TRANSFORMATIONS                            |
|                                                                   |
|  Original Type:                                                   |
|  interface User { id: string; email: string; age: number; }       |
|                                                                   |
|  [Partial<User>]    -> { id?: string; email?: string; age?: ... } |
|  [Readonly<User>]   -> { readonly id: str; readonly email: ... }  |
|  [Pick<User, "id">] -> { id: string }                             |
|  [Omit<User, "age">]-> { id: string; email: string }              |
|                                                                   |
|  Iterates through keys [K in keyof T] and transforms values!      |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
codeExamples.explanation: Mapped types iterate through the keys of an existing type, applying modifiers or transforming value types.

keyPoints: Mapped types iterate over keys using the syntax [K in keyof T].
Modifiers (+/- readonly, +/- ?) add or remove property flags.
Utility types (Pick, Omit, Partial, Record) are standard mapped types built into TypeScript.
commonMistakes: Attempting to use 'Omit' with keys that do not exist, which compiles silently unless constrained.
Over-using Partial<T> for update payloads, allowing accidental clearing of mandatory identifiers.

sections.heading: 2. Production Entity Patch and Dictionary Utilities
sections.content: In RESTful APIs, `PATCH /users/:id` accepts partial updates, but must NEVER allow the user to modify immutable fields like `id` or `createdAt`. Combining `Omit` and `Partial` enforces this invariant at compile time.

codeExamples.explanation: Demonstrates combining Omit and Partial to enforce strict API security invariants at compile time.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Updated user usr_44 fields: bio, avatarUrl

keyPoints: Omit<T, 'id'> strips immutable properties before Partial makes remaining fields optional.
Record<string, T> is preferred over index signatures ({ [key: string]: T }) for dictionary maps.
commonMistakes: Using Partial<UserEntity> directly for updates, which accidentally permits updating immutable primary keys.

exercises.title: Construct a DeepReadonly Mapped Type
exercises.objective: Write a recursive mapped type DeepReadonly<T> that freezes nested object structures.
exercises.description: Standard Readonly<T> is shallow: nested objects remain mutable. Implement a recursive mapped type DeepReadonly<T> that applies readonly recursively to all nested properties and arrays.
instructions: Use conditional check `T extends Function | boolean | number | string | symbol ? T : ...`.
Recursively map `{ readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }`.
hints: Check if `T extends object`; if so, recursively map `DeepReadonly<T[K]>`, else return `T`.
exercises.submissionRequirements: Complete all checklist items, test assumptions, and document verification rationale.
evaluationCriteria: Addresses the root architectural/technical challenge accurately
Follows defensive industry standards and edge-case validation
exercises.solutionExplanation: Recursive mapped types traverse nested object trees at compile time, guaranteeing deep immutability.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: What does the '-?' modifier do in a TypeScript mapped type?

options.text: It removes optionality, making all properties strictly required.
It removes null values from union types.
It reverses the order of properties.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: The '-?' modifier removes optionality from each property, converting optional fields (x?) into mandatory fields.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: Which utility type should you choose to create an object type mapping a fixed set of HTTP status codes to string descriptions?
knowledgeChecks.explanation: Record<K, T> creates an object type whose property keys are K and property values are T.

recap: Mapped types iterate over keys to transform structures. Built-in utility types (Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick, Omit, Record) form the backbone of modern TypeScript API modeling.
